question: Calculate: \(314\times3\times3\times6\div3\div100=?\) (Answer as a decimal.)
solution:
Multiplication and division by the same nonzero number undo each other, so one factor of \(3\) cancels the division by \(3\). Regrouping the remaining factors gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
314\times3\times3\times6\div3\div100
&=314\times(3\times6)\div100\\
&=314\times18\div100\\
&=5652\div100.
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing by \(100\) moves the decimal point two places to the left, so the answer is \(56.52\).

nodes.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.* Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) *Students need not use formal terms for these properties.

edges.reason: Interpreting a multiplication fact as a product uses the meaning of multiplication; deriving every table fact by repeated addition is not separately mandated.

Three-digit-by-two-digit multiplication uses three-digit-by-one-digit partial products and addition. It need not contain a two-digit-by-two-digit multiplication subproblem, so the earlier layout is preparation.

edges.reason: Larger products motivate shortcuts and supply verification examples. Arrays and table products establish swapping/regrouping independently of a two-digit column method.
edges.scope: verifying multiplication laws on multidigit factors

edges.reason: Addition laws provide familiar names and a structural analogy. Multiplication laws follow directly from arrays/equal groups without applying addition associativity or commutativity as a prior theorem.
